summary:
The Faroe Islands are a self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark. Denmark's national criminal law and document rules extend to the territory; equality and family law are made locally beneath that framework.

Consensual same-sex activity has been legal in the Faroe Islands since 1933, when decriminalisation took effect across the Kingdom of Denmark. The territory set its age of consent for male same-sex relations at 18 and did not follow Denmark's 1977 move to a gender-neutral age of 15 until 1988.

Same-sex marriage was legalised in 2017, later than any other Nordic jurisdiction, after open friction between church and state.

The territory's anti-discrimination statute took effect on 1 January 2007, making the Faroe Islands the last Northern European country to prohibit discrimination and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation. The only criminal penalties in force that touch sexual-orientation hostility sit in that statute: anyone who publicly makes a statement threatening, insulting or degrading a group on account of race, colour, national or ethnic origin, religion or sexual orientation is liable to a fine or to imprisonment for up to two years.

Before that date a visitor or resident had no statutory recourse. In 2006 LGBT activists gathered roughly 20,000 online signatures in a population of about 47,000 demanding an end to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and a registered-partnership law aligned with neighbouring Nordic jurisdictions; the territory had neither at that date.

Violence against openly gay people was documented and, at the time, legally unaddressed. In 2006 the singer, songwriter and radio host Rasmus Rasmussen was severely beaten by five men in Tórshavn and hospitalised shortly after coming out; he and his family then received threatening telephone calls, and police refused to handle the case because no Faroese law banned discrimination against sexual minorities. He was later moved to a psychiatric hospital with severe depression aggravated by the beating, never recovered, and died by suicide in 2012. In 2005 the Norwegian drag group Great Garlic Girls had to run from a gang of young men intent on physically attacking them in Tórshavn; the group had not been assaulted anywhere else on its tour.

Religiously motivated opposition remains prominent in Faroese public life. On 7 September 2010 Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana refused to attend a state banquet for visiting Icelandic Prime Minister Johanna Sigurdardottir and her partner, citing his religion. In July 2015 he demanded that Pride be banned, the event falling two days before the national holiday, and he has repeatedly compared the local LGBT organisation to the Sea Shepherd whale-hunting protesters and urged that the Tórshavn parade be moved out of the town centre; his party remains formally opposed to homosexuality.
tangentialFactors:
Public expression has been a recurring flashpoint. The first Faroese gay pride march, held in 2005, provoked substantial controversy, and in June 2015 Løgting Speaker Jógvan á Lakjuni published a letter to the editor, 'Hvar eru vit á veg?', attacking the national broadcaster Kringvarp Føroya for the space it gave LGBT Føroyar, condemning a drag show at the Nordic House as 'non-culture', and asking whether 'these people do not feel any shame'.

Organised pushback against that hostility is documented. When Jenis av Rana demanded a ban on Pride in 2015, the singer Eivor Pálsdottir publicly urged people to ignore him. Petitioning runs in both directions: an internet petition opened after the 2006 assault on Rasmus Rasmussen collected 20,000 signatures, and eight women in Tórshavn gathered a further 2,000 by email and in shops, tourist centres and gas stations, while a petition against same-sex marriage gathered 1,262 signatures.

The territory's pace of reform lags its neighbours on two documented measures: it was the last Northern European jurisdiction to legislate against sexual-orientation discrimination, doing so in 2007, and it legalised same-sex marriage in 2017 after every other Nordic state had done so.
localsOnly:
Family and equality matters are legislated in Tórshavn rather than Copenhagen, so resident-facing rights such as marriage, adoption and partnership follow Faroese statutes enacted by the Løgting, not Danish acts. Same-sex marriage has been available locally since 2017.

Local campaigning has historically mobilised at a scale unusual for the population: a 2006 petition drew about 20,000 signatures against roughly 47,000 residents, and canvassing by eight women in Tórshavn added about 2,000 more by email and in shops, tourist centres and gas stations. The counter-petition against same-sex marriage drew 1,262 signatures.

Hostile statements by elected representatives are a matter of local record. Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana has pressed for Pride to be relocated or banned and has likened the local LGBT organisation to anti-whaling protesters, and his party remains formally opposed to homosexuality. Løgting Speaker Jógvan á Lakjuni used a 2015 letter to criticise the public broadcaster's coverage and a drag show at the Nordic House.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not address gender recognition, legal document or identity-marker changes for trans people, whether issued by the Faroe Islands or by Denmark, beyond the general statement that Denmark's national document rules extend here. Which specific authority a Faroese-issued document carries, and what a Danish passport issued to a resident shows, is unresolved in this record.

No sourced material covers restroom or facility access, healthcare provision or bans on care, entry and visa screening, or port-of-entry examination of gender presentation.

No data is available on the number of complaints, charges or convictions under the anti-discrimination provision that took effect on 1 January 2007, so its practical enforcement cannot be assessed from these sources.

The extent to which Danish hate-crime sentencing provisions, as distinct from the Faroese statement offence, apply in the territory is not resolved here, nor is partner, next-of-kin or inheritance recognition beyond the 2017 marriage law.
